title: Explain Your Code
bottom_line: Type /explain:explain with code, a file or a question. Claude explains it using only what you know or learned before, then logs the new concepts.

sections.heading: You need only Claude Code, plus an optional IDE

cards.title: git (optional)
cards.text: Used, when present, to name the current project after its repository.

cards.title: A connected IDE (optional)
cards.text: Without an argument, the skills use the code highlighted in the IDE, or the opened file. With no IDE connected, they fall back to the current project.

blocks.title: Settings
blocks.text: None. The plugin has no environment variables and no plugin settings.

terms.definition: The code editor connected to Claude Code, which tells Claude which lines you selected and which file you opened.
A language, framework, tool or project, such as Go, .NET or your codebase.
The topics you know well. Explanations may assume them.
The topics you are learning. Explanations define their concepts before using them.
Plain Markdown notes in ~/.explain_skill/ recording which concepts earlier explanations covered.
A concept that looks familiar but behaves differently.

sections.heading: Type the command with what you want explained

blocks.text: The argument can be a code path, a symbol, a question or a concept. The target can be code, a file, a flow or a concept in the current project. Claude also starts this skill on its own when you ask it to explain, walk through, break down or help you understand something, even if you never say "explain".

blocks.title: What it explains when you give no argument
blocks.caption: Only the most recent selection and the most recent opened file count.

blocks.text: The first line of the answer names the target, for example "Explaining `pool.go:40-58` (your selection)", so you can see which input was used.

blocks.title: What you can ask about
items: Code, an idiom, a language feature, a framework concept, an architecture, or how something in the codebase works.

blocks.title: Questions it is made for
items: "what does this goroutine do"
"how does DI work in this .NET service"
"walk me through the request flow"
"why is this a struct and not a class"

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.code:
/explain:explain-unknown .NET, C#, Go
/explain:explain-known C++, Python
/explain:explain how does internal/worker/pool.go shut down its goroutines?
/explain:explain what is IServiceCollection doing in Program.cs
/explain:explain                  # explain the IDE selection or opened file
/explain:explain-known            # I understand the highlighted code (or, without an IDE: I know this codebase)

sections.heading: The first run asks what you know and want to learn

steps.title: Claude asks two questions
steps.text: In one message: which topics do you want to learn (languages, frameworks, tools, for example ".NET, C#, Go"), and which topics do you already know well (for example "C++, Python")? Then it stops and waits.

steps.title: You answer
steps.text: Claude writes your profile from your answers. It does not guess them from context.

steps.title: Your project joins the learning list
steps.text: If the project is on neither list, it is added to the learning list as "<name> (project)", named after the git repo. Claude tells you this in one line, and that `/explain:explain-known` marks it as known.

steps.title: Your original request is answered
steps.text: Claude then continues with what you asked in the first place.

blocks.title: Why the project counts as a topic
blocks.text: A codebase's components and conventions are as unfamiliar to a newcomer as its language.

sections.heading: Each explanation builds only on what you know

blocks.title: What an explanation may rely on

blocks.text: It is written for an engineer learning an unfamiliar stack, for example a C++/Python developer who is new to Go and .NET. Claude reads your project's actual code and points to places as `path:line`.
If you ask about a pure concept, such as "what is a channel", with no code attached, Claude looks for a real use of it in your project and uses that as the example when one exists.

blocks.title: How new concepts are introduced
items: A small concept is defined inline, in one or two sentences, where it first appears.
A large concept gets a short primer before the main explanation.
Each is compared to the most comparable topic on your known list, and the answer says where the comparison breaks.
If no known topic has an honest comparison, the concept is explained from first principles.
A concept already in the log is mentioned briefly ("the `context.Context` we covered before") instead of being explained again.

blocks.title: False friends it flags, for example
items: Go slices sharing their backing array.
C# `struct` being a value type while `class` is a reference type.
`defer` being function-scoped rather than block-scoped.
`async void` in C#.

sections.heading: The answer comes in up to six parts

rows: The actual explanation, grounded in the project's code with `path:line` references and short code excerpts.
Box-and-arrow art in ASCII or Unicode, inside a code block, about 80 columns wide, with each arrow labelled with what flows along it.
False friends and surprising behavior relevant to this code.
One line listing the concepts being added to the log.
blocks.caption: Parts that add nothing for a specific question are left out.

blocks.title: When a diagram is drawn
items: Drawn for request flows, call chains across layers, ownership or lifetimes, concurrency, startup and registration sequences, and type hierarchies.
Skipped for a single idiom or a one-function answer.
A flow too big for about 40 lines is split into an overview and a zoomed-in diagram.

sections.heading: The log saves what you learned, and you can edit it

before.label: Before an explanation
before.text: A concept you have not been taught yet is defined before it is used.

after.label: After it
after.text: The concept is in the log, so the next explanation refers to it briefly and builds on it.

blocks.title: How the log works for you
items: It is written after the explanation is given, so you never wait on bookkeeping.
Language concepts go under the language's topic. What your project's components do, how modules connect, domain terms and conventions go under the project's topic.
Topics on your known list are not logged.
Everything lives in `~/.explain_skill/` as plain Markdown files. Edit them by hand if you want to correct what the skill thinks you know.
The log can grow large without filling the context window.

blocks.title: Defaults and how to change them
rows: The learning log lives in `~/.explain_skill/`, shared by every project on the machine
Not configurable; edit or delete the files by hand
The current project (its git repo name) is registered as a topic you are learning
`/explain:explain-known` with no argument and no IDE marks it known
Explanations go only as deep as your known topics and the log allow

next_action.text: Run `/explain:explain` with a question about your code, then answer the two first-use questions.
next_action.detail: Your answers set which topics explanations may assume and which they must define.
